doc.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Going solo and the Dizzy Gillespie years
title: Dizzy's last month at the Blue Note and his death
summary: Mance played the trumpet week of Dizzy's 75th birthday month, and recalls Dizzy's last words to him before he died.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Yes he did. He had such a knowledge of the piano. You know he had a knowledge of chords that piano players didn’t have. I mean great, wonderful chords too. And so as I said it was a complete learning process for me. It was just so great. And the last gig he played in New York I was on it. He did a whole month at the Blue Note celebrating his 75th birthday, which he did all year, you know every place he went. But he was the only one, it was unprecedented that anyone would work a month in the Blue Note. But each week was different. The first week I think was the big band, the second week was the saxophone players, mostly the ones that had worked with him, the third one I think was the Latin thing, I’m not sure, but I think that was one of the weeks. And the week that I worked with him, the last week was all the trumpet players. Let’s see, Wynton Marsalis, who else —

Jon Faddis, Claudio Roditi. Roy Hargrove. Every night a different trumpet player. And that album came out and it was called “To Dizzy With Love.” And I had such a ball playing with him. It was like the first time I’d played with him for any length of time since I met the dude, and I was just really turned on because I idolized him so much, I’d learned so much from him. And comping, and the other horn players, I’d do something and he’d turn around and look at me and smile and wink. And so when he died I was in tears because the last thing he told me, at the end of the gig that week, you know I

stopped in his dressing room and said, “Dizzy, thanks for inviting me to do this week, it was really a treat for me.” And he looked at me and grabbed me and hugged me and said, “You’re finally doing it.” You don’t know how much that meant to me. Because he had showed me so much. And he said, “You’re doing it, just keep on.” That was the last thing he said to me. He said, “See you next time.” There wasn’t a next time. In fact that’s when he got ill, when he left New York then and he went out to the coast and I think he passed out or something, and died of pancreatic cancer.
Well it’s great that they had that month for him and you were involved.
It is. I don’t know if they released every week, I know I think the saxophone players they released, and the trumpet players. They might come out with them, you know they might hold them back.
